analysis.one_liner: Blocks a 2018 rule letting states weaken protections for people with preexisting conditions.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 230-183 in May 2019, but the Senate never voted on it, and the rule it would have blocked stayed in effect until that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2018, the Trump administration issued guidance loosening how states can get waivers from Affordable Care Act rules. The guidance allowed states to substitute skimpy plans — short-term plans and association health plans — for comprehensive coverage, and to judge whether coverage is adequate based on projections rather than actual enrollment. This bill would have thrown that guidance out and barred the agencies from issuing anything substantially like it, keeping waiver standards closer to the stricter 2015 rules and preserving protections for the roughly one in four Americans with a preexisting condition.
analysis.who_benefits: People with preexisting health conditions — about one in four Americans, including those with disabilities and opioid use disorders — who would otherwise face plans that charge them more, exclude their care, or skimp on benefits like maternity and mental health coverage. It also protects everyone enrolled in comprehensive marketplace coverage, because letting healthier people shift into cheaper skimpy plans drives premiums up for those who stay.

how_it_helps.text: Nullifies the October 2018 'State Relief and Empowerment Waivers' guidance and bars the HHS and Treasury Secretaries from implementing or enforcing it or issuing substantially similar guidance [S4][S5].

The guidance had redefined acceptable coverage under state waivers to include short-term, limited-duration plans and association health plans, which can discriminate against people with preexisting conditions [S2][S3][S5].

The bill specifically bars waiver actions that would reduce coverage of essential health benefits including maternity and newborn care, reduce availability or affordability of coverage for people with substance use disorders, or raise premiums for people with preexisting conditions [S5].
The bill leaves intact state waivers that establish reinsurance programs that lower premiums and protect people with preexisting conditions [S5].

It requires the Government Accountability Office to report within a year on how many people would have been expected to lose coverage, and the effect on mental health treatment, under the 2018 guidance [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Insurers selling short-term, limited-duration plans and association health plans, which rely on the loosened waiver standards to sell cheaper plans that exclude or charge more for preexisting conditions. States seeking broader flexibility to redesign their insurance markets under the 2018 standards also lose a pathway, and the federal agencies lose discretion they had claimed.

drawbacks.text: The bill is narrow: it strikes down one guidance document rather than writing the protections into permanent law, so a future administration's guidance, if not 'substantially similar,' could still loosen waiver standards [S5].

Opponents argued it blocks state innovation: the 2018 guidance was framed as giving states flexibility to experiment with coverage designs, and the bill freezes the agencies' interpretation of waiver standards [S2][S3].

Short-term and association plans do offer lower premiums to healthy people who buy them; limiting those plans keeps coverage more affordable for the sick but removes a cheaper option for the healthy, and critics of the bill pointed to this tradeoff in the floor debate over the Republican motion to recommit [S8].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection for people with preexisting conditions is real: the 2018 guidance would have let states count short-term and association plans — which can deny or price out sick people — as satisfying waiver standards, and would have judged adequacy on projections rather than actual enrollment. The cost is some loss of state flexibility to experiment, and the bill's narrow scope means it protects by locking out one guidance document rather than by writing permanent standards. On balance, the bill trades modest flexibility for protection of roughly a quarter of Americans with health conditions, and states that wanted to genuinely lower premiums could still use reinsurance waivers, which the bill expressly preserves [S5].

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it in May 2019, but the Senate placed it on its calendar and never brought it up for a vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced in February 2019 by Rep. Ann Kuster and referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees [S1][S7].
The Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee forwarded it to the full committee on a 19-13 vote in March, and the full committee ordered it reported by voice vote in April [S7].
The House passed it 230-183 with 1 present on May 9, 2019: 226 of 234 voting Democrats voted yes and zero voted no, while 183 of 197 voting Republicans voted no and only 4 Republicans voted yes [S8].

Before final passage, Republicans' motion to recommit with instructions — which would have added a provision prohibiting HHS from waiving preexisting-condition protections — failed 182-231, with all 182 yes votes from Republicans [S8].

The Senate received the bill on May 14, 2019, read it twice, and placed it on the Senate calendar under General Orders, where it remained with no vote until the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5][S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insurers selling short-term and association health plans kept the market opening the 2018 guidance created, and states favoring the looser waiver standards kept that flexibility, because the guidance the bill would have nullified remained in effect. People with preexisting conditions in states that might have used the guidance got no protection from Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Short-term plan insurers and looser-waiver states

industries.industry: Short-term, limited-duration and association health plan insurers
industries.note: These plans profit by charging healthy people less and excluding or surcharging people with preexisting conditions; the 2018 guidance opened a way for states to count them as adequate coverage, and the bill closes that path. Their business model depends on skimming healthy enrollees, which raises costs for everyone left in comprehensive coverage.

By blocking waivers that would shift enrollees into skimpy plans, the bill keeps the comprehensive-coverage risk pool intact and slows premium increases on marketplace plans. These insurers keep their customer base, and the protection for consumers and for the insurers' enrollment run in the same direction here.

industries.industry: State governments seeking ACA waiver flexibility
industries.note: States lose the loosened 2018 standards for redesigning their markets, though the bill expressly preserves reinsurance waivers that lower premiums while protecting preexisting-condition coverage.
